clues: This New England colony was founded in 1636 by a minister banished from Massachusetts.

explanation: Roger Williams founded Rhode Island in 1636 as a haven for religious freedom and separation of church and state.

trap_notes.b: Thomas Hooker founded Connecticut in 1636, not Roger Williams.
trap_notes.c: New Hampshire began as coastal fishing settlements in the 1620s.
trap_notes.d: Massachusetts Bay was the Puritan colony that banished Roger Williams.

clues: Colonial delegates met in New York in 1754 to discuss defense against France.

clues: King George III issued this royal order right after the Seven Years' War.

trap_notes.c: The 1767 Townshend Acts taxed imported glass, lead, paint, paper, and tea.

trap_notes.d: John Dickinson wrote Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania in 1767.

clues: Western Pennsylvania farmers protested a 1791 federal excise tax in 1794.

trap_notes.d: The Transcontinental Railroad was completed later in 1869 at Promontory, Utah.

clues: Organized in July 1848 by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott.
Delegates issued a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the 1776 Declaration.

explanation: The 1848 Seneca Falls Convention in New York marked the birth of the organized U.S. women's suffrage movement.

trap_notes.c: The Hartford Convention (1814) was a Federalist protest against the War of 1812.
trap_notes.d: The Annapolis Convention (1786) was an early trade meeting before the Constitution.

clues: Fought over three days in July 1863, it was the Civil War's bloodiest battle.

Irish and Chinese crews laid track across plains, deserts, and the Sierra Nevada.

trap_notes.c: The Erie Canal was a New York waterway completed in 1825.

clues: Passed in 1887, this federal law aimed to assimilate Native Americans into farming.

clues: Founded in 1889 in a working-class immigrant neighborhood on Chicago's West Side.

trap_notes.d: Seneca Falls hosted the 1848 women's rights convention in New York.

clues: This 1896 Supreme Court ruling grew out of a challenge to a Louisiana train law.

explanation: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld racial segregation under 'separate but equal' until overturned in 1954.

trap_notes.c: Dred Scott (1857) denied Black citizenship before the Civil War.
trap_notes.d: Loving v. Virginia (1967) struck down bans on interracial marriage.

clues: This brief 1898 conflict followed the explosion of the USS Maine in Havana Harbor.

explanation: The 1898 Spanish-American War ended Spain's New World empire and made the U.S. an overseas colonial power.

trap_notes.c: The War of 1812 was fought against Great Britain.
trap_notes.d: The Philippine-American War (1899–1902) followed the treaty ending the 1898 war.

clues: British intelligence intercepted and decoded this secret message in January 1917.

explanation: Combined with German unrestricted submarine warfare, the 1917 Zimmermann Telegram spurred Congress to declare war.

trap_notes.c: The Atlantic Charter (1941) was a WWII statement by FDR and Churchill.
trap_notes.d: The Treaty of Versailles (1919) formally ended World War I.

clues: This demographic shift reshaped American cities between World War I and 1970.

explanation: The Great Migration transformed politics, labor, and culture in cities like Chicago, Detroit, New York, and Los Angeles.

trap_notes.b: The Exoduster Movement was a smaller 1879 migration of Black families to Kansas.
trap_notes.c: The Dust Bowl Migration moved Plains farmers westward in the 1930s.
trap_notes.d: Post-WWII suburbanization moved mostly white middle-class families outside cities.
trap_notes.default: Six million Black Americans moving from the South to northern/western cities = Great Migration.

clues: Severe drought and overplowing stripped topsoil across the Great Plains in the 1930s.
Massive black dust storms buried barns and ruined farms from Texas to Nebraska.
Thousands of displaced 'Okie' families drove west along Route 66 toward California.

explanation: The 1930s Dust Bowl combined drought and poor farming practices, prompting New Deal soil conservation programs.

trap_notes.b: The Panic of 1893 was a railroad and banking depression in the 1890s.
trap_notes.c: Teapot Dome was a 1920s oil-lease bribery scandal under President Harding.
trap_notes.d: The Great Mississippi Flood occurred earlier in 1927.
trap_notes.default: 1930s + Great Plains drought + 'Okie' migration to California = Dust Bowl.

clues: Passed in 1935, this New Deal law created a permanent federal safety net.
It introduced payroll taxes paid by workers and employers to fund benefits.
It established old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, and aid for dependent children.

explanation: The 1935 Social Security Act became the cornerstone of the modern American social safety net.

trap_notes.d: The 1938 Fair Labor Standards Act set the federal minimum wage and 40-hour week.

clues: Passed in March 1941, this law moved the U.S. away from strict neutrality.

It let the U.S. supply weapons, ships, and food to Britain and later the USSR.
prompt: Which World War II policy do these clues identify?
explanation: The 1941 Lend-Lease Act made the United States the 'arsenal of democracy' before entering WWII.

trap_notes.b: The Marshall Plan (1948) rebuilt Western Europe after WWII ended.
trap_notes.c: The Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930) raised import duties during the Great Depression.
trap_notes.d: The Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928) was an interwar treaty renouncing war.
trap_notes.default: March 1941 + garden hose analogy + war aid to Britain = Lend-Lease Act.

clues: In June 1948, the Soviet Union cut off all rail, road, and canal routes to a divided city.
For nearly a year, Allied cargo planes landed every few minutes with food and coal.
The operation broke the blockade without firing a shot and kept West Berlin free.

explanation: The 1948–1949 Berlin Airlift supplied over two million West Berliners until Stalin lifted the blockade.

trap_notes.b: The Cuban Missile Crisis was a 1962 nuclear standoff in the Caribbean.
trap_notes.c: D-Day was the June 1944 Allied landing in Normandy, France.
trap_notes.d: The Berlin Wall fell much later in November 1989.
trap_notes.default: 1948 Soviet blockade + Allied supply planes = Berlin Airlift.

clues: Proposed by Secretary of State George Marshall in 1947 and launched in 1948.
The U.S. sent over thirteen billion dollars in food, machinery, and loans to Europe.
It rebuilt Western European economies and weakened communist appeal after WWII.
prompt: Which Cold War program do these clues identify?
explanation: The Marshall Plan (European Recovery Program) sparked rapid postwar recovery across Western Europe.

trap_notes.b: The Dawes Plan (1924) restructured German reparations after World War I.
trap_notes.c: The Alliance for Progress (1961) was JFK's economic aid program for Latin America.
trap_notes.d: The Peace Corps (1961) sends American volunteers to developing nations.
trap_notes.default: 1948 + $13 billion + Western European recovery = Marshall Plan.

clues: This 381-day protest began in December 1955 after Rosa Parks was arrested.
Black residents formed carpools and walked miles rather than ride segregated transit.
Led by a young Martin Luther King Jr., it ended with a Supreme Court desegregation ruling.

explanation: The 1955–1956 Montgomery Bus Boycott proved mass nonviolent protest could win legal and social change.

trap_notes.c: The Freedom Rides tested interstate bus desegregation in 1961.
trap_notes.d: The Selma voting rights marches took place in 1965.
trap_notes.default: 1955 + Rosa Parks + Martin Luther King Jr. + 381 days = Montgomery Bus Boycott.

clues: U.S. spy planes spotted Soviet nuclear launch sites ninety miles from Florida in 1962.

Thirteen tense days ended when Khrushchev withdrew the missiles and the U.S. pledged no invasion.

explanation: The October 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis brought the superpowers to the brink of nuclear war before diplomacy prevailed.

trap_notes.b: The Bay of Pigs was a failed 1961 CIA-backed exile landing in Cuba.
trap_notes.c: The Suez Crisis occurred in Egypt in 1956.
trap_notes.d: A U-2 spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960.
trap_notes.default: October 1962 + Soviet missiles in Cuba + naval blockade = Cuban Missile Crisis.

clues: President Kennedy proposed this landmark bill in 1963, and Lyndon Johnson signed it in 1964.
It outlawed segregation in hotels, restaurants, theaters, and other public places.
Title VII also banned job discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.

explanation: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 dismantled legal Jim Crow segregation in public accommodations and employment.

trap_notes.b: The 1965 Voting Rights Act focused specifically on ballot access and literacy tests.
trap_notes.c: The 1968 Fair Housing Act barred discrimination in renting or selling homes.
trap_notes.d: The 1963 Equal Pay Act addressed gender wage gaps.
trap_notes.default: 1964 + public accommodations + Title VII job protections = Civil Rights Act of 1964.

clues: Passed as part of the Education Amendments of 1972 and championed by Patsy Mink.
It bars sex discrimination in any school or college receiving federal funds.

explanation: Title IX opened academic programs and athletics equally to women at federally funded schools and universities.

trap_notes.b: The Equal Rights Amendment was a proposed constitutional amendment, not a 1972 school law.
trap_notes.c: The 1965 Higher Education Act created federal student grants and loans.
trap_notes.d: Head Start (1965) provides early childhood education for low-income families.
trap_notes.default: 1972 + federally funded schools + women's sports equity = Title IX.

clues: Founded in California in the 1960s by Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta.
It used nonviolent strikes, fasts, and a nationwide table-grape boycott.
It won better pay, clean drinking water, and safer pesticide rules for migrant harvesters.
prompt: Which labor organization do these clues identify?
explanation: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta led the United Farm Workers in winning landmark contracts for agricultural workers.

trap_notes.b: The Knights of Labor was a 19th-century national industrial union.
trap_notes.c: The CIO organized factory workers in the 1930s and merged with the AFL in 1955.
trap_notes.d: The AFT represents public school teachers and staff, not farmworkers.
trap_notes.default: Cesar Chavez + Dolores Huerta + grape boycott = United Farm Workers.

prompt: Which region had the highest percentage growth from 1700 to 1770?
explanation: The Middle Colonies grew more than tenfold (from 53,000 to 556,000), a faster rate than New England or the South.

trap_notes.b: New England grew roughly sixfold, slower than the Middle Colonies' tenfold rise.
trap_notes.c: The Southern Colonies had the largest total population, not the fastest percentage rate.
trap_notes.d: The Southern Colonies grew faster than New England in both numbers and percentage.
trap_notes.default: Compare ending to starting size: 556 / 53 is over 10x in the Middle Colonies.

stimulus.title: Top Colonial Exports to Britain (Annual Avg.)

prompt: What does the table show about colonial exports to Britain?

options.text: Southern plantation crops dominated British colonial trade
New England fish earned more than Middle Colony grain
Wheat and flour made up over half of all exports
All three regions shipped equal shares to Britain

explanation: Tobacco and rice from the Southern Colonies accounted for 70 percent of colonial export value to Britain.

trap_notes.b: Middle Colonies' grain (18%) exceeded New England's fish and timber (12%).
trap_notes.c: Wheat and flour were 18% of exports, far less than half.
trap_notes.d: Shares varied sharply from 12% to 70% across the three regions.
trap_notes.default: 70% of export value came from Southern tobacco and rice.

prompt: What conclusion does the ratification table best support?

options.text: Large states like Massachusetts and Virginia were closely divided
Every state ratified the Constitution by a unanimous vote
Virginia rejected the Constitution before voting a second time
Delaware opposed the Constitution until a Bill of Rights passed

explanation: While small Delaware voted 30–0 in favor, Massachusetts and Virginia passed ratification by narrow margins.

trap_notes.b: Only Delaware was unanimous among these three; Massachusetts and Virginia had strong opposition.
trap_notes.c: Virginia ratified 89–79 on its first convention vote in June 1788.
trap_notes.d: Delaware was the very first state to ratify, voting 30–0.
trap_notes.default: Massachusetts (187–168) and Virginia (89–79) show fierce debate in large states.

stimulus.title: U.S. Trade During Embargo Act (Millions USD)

prompt: How did the 1807 Embargo Act affect U.S. trade in 1808?

options.text: Both exports and imports fell sharply by more than half
Exports doubled while imports stayed nearly flat
The United States achieved a large trade surplus
Imports dropped to zero while exports rose slightly

explanation: Jefferson's 1807 Embargo Act devastated American shipping, slashing exports from $108M to $22M in 1808.

trap_notes.b: Both exports and imports plunged in 1808 rather than rising.
trap_notes.c: Imports ($57M) still exceeded exports ($22M) in 1808.
trap_notes.d: Imports fell to $57M, not zero, and exports dropped dramatically.
trap_notes.default: Exports fell 80% ($108M to $22M) and imports fell nearly 60% ($139M to $57M).

prompt: What trend does the table illustrate between 1820 and 1860?

options.text: Booming cotton output grew alongside the enslaved population
Rising cotton production reduced demand for enslaved labor
Cotton output peaked in 1840 and declined by 1860
The enslaved population fell after the cotton gin spread

explanation: As cotton output surged over tenfold from 1820 to 1860, slavery expanded across the Deep South.

trap_notes.b: Both cotton bales and the enslaved population rose steadily together.
trap_notes.c: Cotton output nearly tripled between 1840 and 1860.
trap_notes.d: The enslaved population more than doubled from 1.5M to 4.0M.
trap_notes.default: Cotton bales (335k to 3.84M) and enslaved people (1.5M to 4.0M) rose together.

prompt: What strategic advantage for the Union does the 1860 row show?

options.text: The North held more than twice the South's rail mileage
The South built more track than the North during the 1850s
Southern rail lines equaled northern mileage by 1860
Rail construction stopped in the North after 1850

explanation: With 21,600 miles of track compared to 9,000 in the South, the Union could move troops and supplies far faster.

trap_notes.b: The North added 14,800 miles in the 1850s, while the South added 6,800 miles.
trap_notes.c: Southern mileage in 1860 (9,000) was less than half of northern mileage (21,600).
trap_notes.d: Northern mileage more than tripled between 1850 and 1860.
trap_notes.default: In 1860, the North had 21,600 rail miles vs. 9,000 in the South.

prompt: Which factor best explains the 1841–1850 jump shown in the table?

options.text: The Irish Potato Famine drove mass migration to U.S. cities
The Homestead Act gave free farms to European arrivals
Congress lifted the Chinese Exclusion Act in 1845
World War I displaced millions of German refugees

explanation: Crop failure and starvation in Ireland during the late 1840s caused immigration to nearly triple.

trap_notes.b: The Homestead Act was passed later in 1862.
trap_notes.c: The Chinese Exclusion Act was passed in 1882 and repealed in 1943.
trap_notes.d: World War I occurred much later in 1914–1918.
trap_notes.default: 1841–1850 surge + Ireland as top origin = Irish Potato Famine.

prompt: How did Lincoln win 180 electoral votes with under 40% of the vote?

options.text: He carried populous northern states while rivals split votes
He won every southern state by a narrow popular margin
Congress awarded him bonus electoral votes after secession
Douglas dropped out and gave his electors to Lincoln

explanation: Because the Democratic Party split north and south, Lincoln swept high-electoral northern states.

trap_notes.b: Lincoln was not even on the ballot in most Deep South states.
trap_notes.c: The 180 electoral votes came directly from state results, not congressional bonuses.
trap_notes.d: Douglas stayed in the race and won 12 electoral votes.
trap_notes.default: Sweeping populous free states gave Lincoln an Electoral College majority with 39.8%.

prompt: Which challenge for the Confederacy is clearest from the table?

options.text: Severe shortages in industrial manufacturing and weapons
Lack of farmland to grow cotton or food crops
Having a larger civilian population than the Union
Too many weapons factories competing for workers

explanation: With only 10% of factory output and 3% of firearms production, the South struggled to supply a long war.

trap_notes.b: The table measures population, factories, and firearms, not agricultural land.
trap_notes.c: The Confederacy held only 29% of the nation's population, including enslaved people.
trap_notes.d: The Confederacy produced just 3% of the nation's firearms.
trap_notes.default: 90% of factories and 97% of firearms belonged to the Union in 1861.

prompt: What caused the sharp drop in Black voter registration by 1890?

options.text: State disenfranchisement laws like poll taxes and literacy tests
Ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870
Passage of the federal Voting Rights Act
Expansion of Freedmen's Bureau schools across rural counties

explanation: Mississippi's 1890 constitution used poll taxes and biased literacy tests to strip Black citizens of the vote.

trap_notes.b: The Fifteenth Amendment protected voting rights rather than taking them away.
trap_notes.c: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 later banned literacy tests.
trap_notes.d: Freedmen's Bureau schools expanded literacy during Reconstruction, not disenfranchisement.
trap_notes.default: Mississippi's 1890 poll tax and literacy test cut Black registration by over 85%.

prompt: What does the table show about U.S. steel between 1870 and 1900?

options.text: Output surged over a hundredfold during industrial expansion
Steel production fell after Carnegie combined mines and mills
Most steel growth happened before the Bessemer process arrived
Output leveled off at five million tons by 1900

explanation: Bessemer converters and Carnegie's vertical integration turned the U.S. into the world's top steel producer.

trap_notes.b: Production jumped from 4.8 million to 11.4 million tons after 1890.
trap_notes.c: The Bessemer process and open-hearth furnaces drove the huge surge after 1870.
trap_notes.d: Output more than doubled between 1890 and 1900, reaching 11.4 million tons.
trap_notes.default: U.S. steel output rose from 0.08M tons in 1870 to 11.4M tons in 1900.

stimulus.title: U.S. Urban vs. Rural Population Share

prompt: What historic milestone did the 1920 U.S. Census mark?

options.text: More Americans lived in cities and towns than in rural areas
Rural farm populations grew faster than urban centers
Factory jobs declined while farming became the top employer
Half of all Americans moved to suburbs outside cities
